claim: Activity-regulated genes (ARGs) are important for neuronal functions like long-term memory.
source: Activity-regulated genes (ARGs) are important for neuronal functions like long-term memory and are well-characterized in mammals but poorly studied in other model organisms like Drosophila.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about ARGs.

claim: ARGs are well-characterized in mammals.
source: Activity-regulated genes (ARGs) are important for neuronal functions like long-term memory and are well-characterized in mammals but poorly studied in other model organisms like Drosophila.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in the field.

claim: ARGs are poorly studied in Drosophila.
source: Activity-regulated genes (ARGs) are important for neuronal functions like long-term memory and are well-characterized in mammals but poorly studied in other model organisms like Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by the introduction which mentions only three genes identified in insects and one genome-wide study from over a decade ago.

claim: Many ARGs are specific to the stimulation paradigm.
source: Surprisingly, many ARGs are specific to the stimulation paradigm and very specific to neuron type.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D showing limited overlap between different stimulation paradigms.

claim: Many ARGs are very specific to neuron type.
source: Surprisingly, many ARGs are specific to the stimulation paradigm and very specific to neuron type.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5A showing limited overlap between different neuron types.

claim: Fly ARGs do not have short gene lengths unlike mammalian immediate early genes (IEGs).
source: In addition and unlike mammalian immediate early genes (IEGs), fly ARGs do not have short gene lengths and are less enriched for transcription factor function.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2C showing that ARGs have longer gene lengths than average genes.

claim: Fly ARGs are less enriched for transcription factor function compared to mammalian IEGs.
source: In addition and unlike mammalian immediate early genes (IEGs), fly ARGs do not have short gene lengths and are less enriched for transcription factor function.
evidence: This is supported by the GO analysis in Figure 1D and Table 1 showing weaker enrichment compared to mammals.

claim: The transcription start sites (TSS) of ARGs do not change with neural firing.
source: Chromatin assays using ATAC-sequencing show that the transcription start sites (TSS) of ARGs do not change with neural firing but are already accessible prior to stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The TSS of ARGs are already accessible prior to stimulation.
source: Chromatin assays using ATAC-sequencing show that the transcription start sites (TSS) of ARGs do not change with neural firing but are already accessible prior to stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6D comparing baseline accessibility.

claim: Immediate-early genes (IEGs) are induced rapidly and transiently without de novo protein synthesis in mammalian neurons.
source: Upon stimulation, immediate-early genes (IEGs) are induced rapidly and transiently without de novo protein synthesis in mammalian neurons (Fowler et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fowler et al., 2011.

claim: Activity-dependent gene regulation is important for converting transient stimuli into long-term changes.
source: This activity-dependent gene regulation is important as it affects the ability of an animal to convert transient stimuli into long-term changes (Huh et al., 2000; Kandel, 2001; Nestler, 2001; Spitzer et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hundreds of IEGs have been identified in mammals since the discovery of c-fos in 1986.
source: Hundreds of IEGs, including those specific to tissues and stimulation paradigms, have been identified in mammals since the discovery of the first neuronal IEG, c-fos, by Greenberg and his colleagues in 1986 (Greenberg et al., 1986; Herschman, 1991; Spiegel et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to historical and review papers.

claim: c-fos was the first neuronal IEG discovered by Greenberg and colleagues in 1986.
source: Hundreds of IEGs, including those specific to tissues and stimulation paradigms, have been identified in mammals since the discovery of the first neuronal IEG, c-fos, by Greenberg and his colleagues in 1986 (Greenberg et al., 1986; Herschman, 1991; Spiegel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Greenberg et al., 1986.

claim: IEG expression is induced within an hour with large amplitudes (over 10 fold).
source: Expression of these IEGs are induced within an hour, usually with big amplitudes (over 10 fold), and many IEGs are shared between different types of neurons (Spiegel et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spiegel et al., 2014.

claim: Many IEGs are shared between different types of neurons.
source: Expression of these IEGs are induced within an hour, usually with big amplitudes (over 10 fold), and many IEGs are shared between different types of neurons (Spiegel et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spiegel et al., 2014.

claim: IEGs are highly enriched for transcription factors.
source: Functionally, these IEGs are highly enriched for transcription factors, which subsequently trigger a secondary transcriptional response (Spiegel et al., 2014; West and Greenberg, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Spiegel et al., 2014 and West and Greenberg, 2011.

claim: IEGs trigger a secondary transcriptional response.
source: Functionally, these IEGs are highly enriched for transcription factors, which subsequently trigger a secondary transcriptional response (Spiegel et al., 2014; West and Greenberg, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Secondary response genes (SRGs) take longer to induce than IEGs, with a typical assay time of 6 hr post-stimulation.
source: The secondary response genes (SRGs) in contrast take longer to induce (a typical assay is 6 hr post-stimulation), are involved in many different processes, are more neuron-specific and function at least in part to promote neuron survival, dendritic morphogenesis and regulate synapse formation (Bloodgood et al., 2013; Hong et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: SRGs are more neuron-specific than IEGs.
source: The secondary response genes (SRGs) in contrast take longer to induce (a typical assay is 6 hr post-stimulation), are involved in many different processes, are more neuron-specific and function at least in part to promote neuron survival, dendritic morphogenesis and regulate synapse formation (Bloodgood et al., 2013; Hong et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: SRGs function to promote neuron survival, dendritic morphogenesis and regulate synapse formation.
source: The secondary response genes (SRGs) in contrast take longer to induce (a typical assay is 6 hr post-stimulation), are involved in many different processes, are more neuron-specific and function at least in part to promote neuron survival, dendritic morphogenesis and regulate synapse formation (Bloodgood et al., 2013; Hong et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Not all IEGs respond to all types of stimulations.
source: Not all IEGs respond to all types of stimulations, even the most robust ones like c-fos, Egr1 and Arc (Bepari et al., 2012; Fields et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Different stimulation paradigm-dependent Ca2+ entry routes initiate different downstream pathways and lead to induction of distinct IEGs.
source: For example, different stimulation paradigm-dependent Ca2+ entry routes initiate different downstream pathways and lead to induction of distinct IEGs (West and Greenberg, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to West and Greenberg, 2011.

claim: Stimulations other than neural firing like growth factors also induce IEG expression.
source: Stimulations other than neural firing like growth factors also induce IEG expression, many of which are the same as those induced with neural firing (Jones et al., 1988; Tullai et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Tullai et al. divided PDGF-induced IEGs into primary response genes (PRGs) and delayed response genes (DRGs).
source: Depending on the induction dynamics, Tullai et al. divided the platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)-induced IEGs in human T98G glioblastoma cells into primary response genes (PRGs) and delayed response genes (DRGs).
evidence: This statement refers to work by Tullai et al.

claim: PRGs and DRGs show dramatic differences in functions, gene lengths, chromatin accessibility and RNA polymerase II occupancy at promoter regions.
source: Dramatic differences were shown between the two categories in terms of their functions, gene lengths, chromatin accessibility and RNA polymerase II occupancy at promoter regions (Fowler et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2010; Tullai et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: PRGs are optimized for rapid induction with shorter gene length and more permissive chromatin at promoters.
source: PRGs are usually optimized for rapid induction (such as shorter gene length and more permissive chromatin at promoters), whereas DRGs are not different from other genes in the genome.
evidence: This statement is based on cited literature.

claim: DRGs are not different from other genes in the genome.
source: PRGs are usually optimized for rapid induction (such as shorter gene length and more permissive chromatin at promoters), whereas DRGs are not different from other genes in the genome.
evidence: This statement is based on cited literature.

claim: PRGs and DRGs are induced independent of protein-synthesis (cycloheximide-insensitive).
source: Notably, PRGs and DRGs are induced independent of protein-synthesis ('cycloheximide-insensitive'), whereas SRGs are protein-synthesis dependent ('cycloheximide-sensitive').
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: SRGs are protein-synthesis dependent (cycloheximide-sensitive).
source: Notably, PRGs and DRGs are induced independent of protein-synthesis ('cycloheximide-insensitive'), whereas SRGs are protein-synthesis dependent ('cycloheximide-sensitive').
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Only three genes have been identified as responding to increased neural activity in insects: kakusei, stripe, and hr38.
source: Only three genes to date have been identified as responding to increased neural activity in insects: kakusei (in honey bee), stripe (abbreviated as sr, in honey bee) and hr38 (in silkmoth and the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster) (Fujita et al., 2013; Kiya et al., 2007; Lutz and Robinson, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Only one genome-wide study using microarrays had been performed more than a decade ago to identify seizure-induced ARGs from fly heads.
source: Moreover, only one genome-wide study using microarrays had been performed more than a decade ago to identify seizure-induced ARGs from fly heads (Guan et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Guan et al., 2005.

claim: Elav-GAL4 was used to drive expression of UAS-ChR2-XXL to artificially fire neurons.
source: To identify ARGs in fly neurons in a genome-wide manner, the pan-neuronal driver Elav-GAL4 was used to drive expression of UAS-ChR2-XXL, to artificially fire neurons by illuminating flies with a blue LED (Dawydow et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: A 30 s 10 Hz LED exposure was sufficient to induce a uniform seizure within seconds.
source: A 30 s 10 Hz LED exposure was sufficient to induce a uniform seizure within seconds, and all flies were able to recover within 15 min.
evidence: This describes an observation from the experiment.

claim: All flies were able to recover within 15 min after LED stimulation.
source: A 30 s 10 Hz LED exposure was sufficient to induce a uniform seizure within seconds, and all flies were able to recover within 15 min.
evidence: This describes an observation from the experiment.

claim: 96 genes show significant increases at 60 min with p-value < 0.01 in UAS-ChR2-XXL flies.
source: 96 genes show significant increases in 60 min with p-value < 0.01 of both exact test and general linear model (GLM) in UAS-ChR2-XXL flies (N = 3 biological replicas); very few genes show significant decreases (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct result from the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: hr38 and sr rank #1 and #2 among ChR2-XXL-induced ARGs.
source: Ranking #1 and #2 are the previously identified insect IEGs hr38 and sr, with a 90- and a 10- fold increase respectively, suggesting the stimulation paradigm is sufficient to fire neurons in the brain (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1C and source data.

claim: hr38 shows a 90-fold increase with ChR2-XXL stimulation.
source: Ranking #1 and #2 are the previously identified insect IEGs hr38 and sr, with a 90- and a 10- fold increase respectively, suggesting the stimulation paradigm is sufficient to fire neurons in the brain (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1C.

claim: sr shows a 10-fold increase with ChR2-XXL stimulation.
source: Ranking #1 and #2 are the previously identified insect IEGs hr38 and sr, with a 90- and a 10- fold increase respectively, suggesting the stimulation paradigm is sufficient to fire neurons in the brain (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1C.

claim: Four genes were up-regulated in control flies with LED exposure.
source: The 30 s LED exposure affected many fewer genes in control flies: four were up-regulated, and three down-regulated with p-values<0.01 by both statistical tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, N = 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Three genes were down-regulated in control flies with LED exposure.
source: The 30 s LED exposure affected many fewer genes in control flies: four were up-regulated, and three down-regulated with p-values<0.01 by both statistical tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, N = 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CG13055, hsp23 and hsromega are labeled as light-induced genes.
source: 3 of the four up-regulated genes, CG13055, hsp23 and hsromega, had induction amplitudes statistically indistinguishable from those of the UAS-ChR2-XXL flies and are therefore labeled as light-induced genes in Figure 1—source data 1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on the comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PolII transcription factor activity is the most enriched function among ChR2-XXL-induced ARGs.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis using GOrilla (http://cbl-gorilla.cs.technion.ac.il/) on the 96 ARG genes shows that polII transcription factor activity is the most enriched function with a P-value of 1.29E-4 computed according to the mHG or HG model, followed by steroid hormone receptor activity and MAP kinase activity (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: HR38 shows 67% identity to nuclear receptor subfamily four group A member 2 (NR4A2).
source: Several of these induced transcription factors encode proteins with high sequence identity to well-known mammalian IEGs: HR38 shows 67% identity to nuclear receptor subfamily four group A member 2 (NR4A2); SR has 82% identity to early growth response protein 3 (EGR3); CBT is 61% identical to Krueppel-like factor 11 (KLF11).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: SR has 82% identity to early growth response protein 3 (EGR3).
source: Several of these induced transcription factors encode proteins with high sequence identity to well-known mammalian IEGs: HR38 shows 67% identity to nuclear receptor subfamily four group A member 2 (NR4A2); SR has 82% identity to early growth response protein 3 (EGR3); CBT is 61% identical to Krueppel-like factor 11 (KLF11).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: CBT is 61% identical to Krueppel-like factor 11 (KLF11).
source: Several of these induced transcription factors encode proteins with high sequence identity to well-known mammalian IEGs: HR38 shows 67% identity to nuclear receptor subfamily four group A member 2 (NR4A2); SR has 82% identity to early growth response protein 3 (EGR3); CBT is 61% identical to Krueppel-like factor 11 (KLF11).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The levels of most ARGs continue to increase until 60 min post-stimulation.
source: The levels of most ARGs continue to increase until the last time point assayed (60 min); only a few transcripts like cbt (2.6 kb) reach maximum expression levels at 30 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on the heat map in Figure 2A and expression profiles in Figure 2B.

claim: cbt reaches maximum expression levels at 30 min.
source: The levels of most ARGs continue to increase until the last time point assayed (60 min); only a few transcripts like cbt (2.6 kb) reach maximum expression levels at 30 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The average ARG gene is longer than that of all annotated genes.
source: Surprisingly, the average ARG gene is longer than that of all annotated genes as well as of all genes expressed in neurons (Figure 2C, gene annotation obtained from FlyBase (ftp://ftp.flybase.net/genomes/dmel/dmel_r5.2_FB2007_01/fasta)).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C comparing gene length distributions.

claim: The average ARG gene is longer than all genes expressed in neurons.
source: Surprisingly, the average ARG gene is longer than that of all annotated genes as well as of all genes expressed in neurons (Figure 2C, gene annotation obtained from FlyBase (ftp://ftp.flybase.net/genomes/dmel/dmel_r5.2_FB2007_01/fasta)).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C comparing gene length distributions.

claim: hr38 is ~31 kb long.
source: This is true even for some of the most robust ARGs; hr38 is ~31 kb long, sr spans ~ 11 kb, CG8910 is ~21 kb and CG11221 is ~13 kb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: sr spans ~11 kb.
source: This is true even for some of the most robust ARGs; hr38 is ~31 kb long, sr spans ~ 11 kb, CG8910 is ~21 kb and CG11221 is ~13 kb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CG8910 is ~21 kb.
source: This is true even for some of the most robust ARGs; hr38 is ~31 kb long, sr spans ~ 11 kb, CG8910 is ~21 kb and CG11221 is ~13 kb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CG11221 is ~13 kb.
source: This is true even for some of the most robust ARGs; hr38 is ~31 kb long, sr spans ~ 11 kb, CG8910 is ~21 kb and CG11221 is ~13 kb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The canonical mammalian IEG c-fos is only ~3.4 kb.
source: In contrast, the canonical mammalian IEGs c-fos and c-jun are only ~ 3.4 kb and ~3.2 kb respectively.
evidence: This is based on known gene structures from mammalian genomes.

claim: The canonical mammalian IEG c-jun is ~3.2 kb.
source: In contrast, the canonical mammalian IEGs c-fos and c-jun are only ~ 3.4 kb and ~3.2 kb respectively.
evidence: This is based on known gene structures from mammalian genomes.

claim: The average gene size of flies is ~9.3 kb.
source: This is despite the fact that the average gene size of flies (~9.3 kb) is considerably smaller than that of mammals (~47 kb for mouse).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation data.

claim: The average gene size of mammals is ~47 kb for mouse.
source: This is despite the fact that the average gene size of flies (~9.3 kb) is considerably smaller than that of mammals (~47 kb for mouse).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation data.

claim: There is a weak anti-correlation between gene length and fold changes at 15 min (FC15/0).
source: To test if gene length affects ARG induction rates, we compared the fold changes of gene expression between 0 and 15 min (FC15/0) relative to gene lengths. There is a weak anti-correlation, suggesting that longer genes are indeed more slowly induced on average (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Longer genes are more slowly induced on average.
source: To test if gene length affects ARG induction rates, we compared the fold changes of gene expression between 0 and 15 min (FC15/0) relative to gene lengths. There is a weak anti-correlation, suggesting that longer genes are indeed more slowly induced on average (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is inferred from the anti-correlation shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The correlation between gene length and fold change disappears when comparing FC60/0.
source: This is not because overall induction amplitudes are smaller for longer genes, since the correlation disappears if fold changes between 0 and 60 min (FC60/0) are compared to gene lengths (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The enhanced transcription of hr38 and sr is obvious at 15 min based on nascent RNA data.
source: Although hr38 and sr mRNA levels peak at 60 min with little or no changes evident at 15 min and even at 30 min (Figure 2F,G), the nascent RNA data indicate that the enhanced transcription of both genes is obvious at the first 15 min time point and peaks at 30 min, 30 min before the peak time of mRNA (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F and 2G comparing nascent RNA and mRNA levels.

claim: The nascent RNA of hr38 and sr peaks at 30 min, 30 min before the mRNA peak.
source: Although hr38 and sr mRNA levels peak at 60 min with little or no changes evident at 15 min and even at 30 min (Figure 2F,G), the nascent RNA data indicate that the enhanced transcription of both genes is obvious at the first 15 min time point and peaks at 30 min, 30 min before the peak time of mRNA (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: For shorter genes like CG14186, there is no delay between nascent and mRNA peak times.
source: For shorter genes such as CG14186 (5.7 kb), the stimulation-induced increases are smaller at the nascent RNA level, presumably because much less time is required for transcription elongation and polyadenylation. More importantly and unlike the longer genes, there is no delay between the nascent and mRNA peak times for the shorter genes (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2H.

claim: 97 genes were induced by dTrpA1 at 60 min but not induced or induced much less robustly in control flies.
source: Hundreds of genes are induced with the dTrpA1 paradigm but many are also robustly heat-induced, i.e., they are also induced in control flies expressing only Elav-GAL4. Nonetheless, 97 genes including hr38 and sr were induced by dTrpA1 at 60 min but not induced or induced much less robustly in the control flies (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and source data.

claim: Only 38 genes were significantly induced by KCl in 60 min.
source: With KCl treatment, only 38 genes were significantly induced in 60 min, and most of them are stress-induced such as heat shock genes (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-seq data in Figure 3—source data 2.

claim: Hr38 and sr were significantly induced by KCl but with much smaller increases (2.5 and 1.5 fold, respectively) compared to other paradigms.
source: Hr38 and sr were also significantly induced by KCl but with much smaller increases (2.5 and 1.5 fold, respectively) compared to the other two paradigms (Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on comparing the fold changes across different paradigms in the source data.

claim: 107 genes were significantly induced by KCl at 90 min.
source: Because many more ARGs (107 genes in total) were significantly induced and had bigger induction amplitudes at 90 min compared to 60 min (Figure 3—source data 3, Figure 3C), this 90 min time point was compared with the other two induction methods.
evidence: This is based on the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C and source data 3.

claim: Only 12 ARGs are shared by all three stimulation paradigms (ChR2-XXL, dTrpA1, and KCl).
source: Only 12 ARGs are shared by all the three paradigms (including hr38 and sr; Figure 3D,E, Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 3D.

claim: 13 genes are shared between dTrpA1 and KCl paradigms.
source: The overlap between the three different pairwise combinations is larger: 13 genes are shared between dTrpA1 (13% of dTrpA1-induced ARGs) and KCl (12% of KCl-induced ARGs), and 24 genes between ChR2-XXL (25% of ChR2-XXL-induced ARGs) and KCl (22% of KCl-induced ARGs).
evidence: This is based on the Venn diagram analysis in Figure 3D.

claim: 24 genes are shared between ChR2-XXL and KCl paradigms.
source: The overlap between the three different pairwise combinations is larger: 13 genes are shared between dTrpA1 (13% of dTrpA1-induced ARGs) and KCl (12% of KCl-induced ARGs), and 24 genes between ChR2-XXL (25% of ChR2-XXL-induced ARGs) and KCl (22% of KCl-induced ARGs).
evidence: This is based on the Venn diagram analysis in Figure 3D.

claim: 35 genes are shared between ChR2-XXL and dTrpA1 paradigms.
source: The largest number (35) and fraction of genes are shared between ChR2-XXL (36% of ChR2-XXL-induced ARGs) and dTrpA1 (36% of dTrpA1-induced ARGs).
evidence: This is based on the Venn diagram analysis in Figure 3D.

claim: pk61c and skl are induced only by ChR2-XXL.
source: For example, pk61c and skl are induced only by ChR2-XXL; CG13054, whereas grass is induced only by dTrpA1; CG13322 and CG10383 are only induced by KCl (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CG13054 and grass are induced only by dTrpA1.
source: For example, pk61c and skl are induced only by ChR2-XXL; CG13054, whereas grass is induced only by dTrpA1; CG13322 and CG10383 are only induced by KCl (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CG13322 and CG10383 are only induced by KCl.
source: For example, pk61c and skl are induced only by ChR2-XXL; CG13054, whereas grass is induced only by dTrpA1; CG13322 and CG10383 are only induced by KCl (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Each brain has about ~120 DA neurons.
source: DA and PDF+ neurons are two distinct populations and serve different functions in flies. Each brain has about ~120 DA neurons and ~16 PDF+ neurons.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Drosophila neuroanatomy.

claim: Each brain has about ~16 PDF+ neurons.
source: DA and PDF+ neurons are two distinct populations and serve different functions in flies. Each brain has about ~120 DA neurons and ~16 PDF+ neurons.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Drosophila neuroanatomy.

claim: Expression profiles from DA and PDF+ neurons are well correlated between replicates (R2 > 0.9).
source: Despite much less starting material than brains, expression profiles from both cell types are well correlated between replicates (R2 > 0.9 between replicates) (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Baseline expression profiles among brains, PDF+ and DA neurons are distinct.
source: In contrast, baseline expression profiles among cells and tissues (brains, PDF+ and DA neurons) are distinct as expected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Act5C is expressed ubiquitously in brains, DA and PDF+ neurons.
source: The housekeeping gene Act5C is expressed ubiquitously in brains, DA and PDF+ neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ple is highly enriched in DA neurons.
source: The DA neuron-enriched transcript ple (encodes tyrosine hydroxylase) and the PDF+ neuron-specific transcript pdf are both highly enriched only in the corresponding neuron types, indicating the correct cell types were collected (Figure 4C) (Budnik and White, 1987; Helfrich‐Förster, 1997).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and supported by citations.

claim: pdf is highly enriched in PDF+ neurons.
source: The DA neuron-enriched transcript ple (encodes tyrosine hydroxylase) and the PDF+ neuron-specific transcript pdf are both highly enriched only in the corresponding neuron types, indicating the correct cell types were collected (Figure 4C) (Budnik and White, 1987; Helfrich‐Förster, 1997).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and supported by citations.

claim: 85 candidate ARGs in DA neurons are significantly induced in dTrpA1 flies but not in control flies.
source: 85 candidate ARGs in DA neurons and 81 in PDF+ neurons are significantly induced in dTrpA1 flies but not in control flies (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5A and source data.

claim: 81 candidate ARGs in PDF+ neurons are significantly induced in dTrpA1 flies but not in control flies.
source: 85 candidate ARGs in DA neurons and 81 in PDF+ neurons are significantly induced in dTrpA1 flies but not in control flies (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5A and source data.

claim: Only six genes are common between all three sources (brains, DA and PDF+ neurons).
source: There was also very limited overlap between the three sets of ARGs: only six genes are in common between all three sources, brains, DA and PDF+ neurons (Figure 5A,B); 11 additional genes are shared between brains and DA neurons; seven between DA and PDF+; and six between brains and PDF+ neurons (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 5A.

claim: Half of the six common genes are among the 12 genes induced by all three stimulation paradigms in brains.
source: Notably, half of the six common genes are among the 12 genes induced by all three stimulation paradigms in brains (CG14186, CG17778 and l(1)G0148, Figure 3E), suggesting that these genes respond to firing in many and perhaps most fly brain neurons (Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This is based on comparing the gene lists from Figure 3E and Figure 5B.

claim: CG13054 and grass are only significantly induced in brains and DA but not PDF+ neurons.
source: For example, CG13054 and grass are only significantly induced in brains and DA but not PDF+ neurons; Mtk and CG8407 are only significantly induced in DA neurons; CG9313 and DAT are exclusively up-regulated in PDF+ neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mtk and CG8407 are only significantly induced in DA neurons.
source: For example, CG13054 and grass are only significantly induced in brains and DA but not PDF+ neurons; Mtk and CG8407 are only significantly induced in DA neurons; CG9313 and DAT are exclusively up-regulated in PDF+ neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CG9313 and DAT are exclusively up-regulated in PDF+ neurons.
source: For example, CG13054 and grass are only significantly induced in brains and DA but not PDF+ neurons; Mtk and CG8407 are only significantly induced in DA neurons; CG9313 and DAT are exclusively up-regulated in PDF+ neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: JhI-21 and CG10863 show changes in sorted DA and PDF+ neurons but smaller or no changes in brains.
source: There are also genes like JhI-21 and CG10863, which show changes in sorted DA and PDF+ neurons but smaller or no changes in brains; this suggests masking/dilution effects in brains (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Almost complete overlap was observed for heat-induced genes across different tissues.
source: In contrast, almost complete overlap was observed for heat-induced genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The TSS and its surrounding region (±250 bp) of all annotated fly genes are more accessible than other regions in the genome.
source: The TSS and its surrounding region (±250 bp) of all annotated fly genes are more accessible than other regions in the genome as expected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 using ATAC-seq data.

claim: The TSS region of ARGs shows enhanced accessibility but does not detectably change with firing.
source: This region of ARGs also shows enhanced accessibility but does not detectably change with firing despite the increase in transcription (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A using ATAC-seq data.

claim: The TSS accessibility of hr38 shows no differences with firing.
source: Even the TSS accessibility of top-ranked ARGs like hr38 (rank #1) and CG7995 (rank #6) shows no differences with firing (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B using ATAC-seq data.

claim: The TSS accessibility of CG7995 shows no differences with firing.
source: Even the TSS accessibility of top-ranked ARGs like hr38 (rank #1) and CG7995 (rank #6) shows no differences with firing (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 using ATAC-seq data.

claim: The TSS of heat shock protein genes possesses less accessible chromatin than that of ARGs at baseline.
source: This is in contrast to the TSS of heat shock protein genes (HSPs), which possesses less accessible chromatin than that of ARGs at baseline but opens substantially by 30 min in both the dTrpA1 and control flies in response to heat (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C using ATAC-seq data.

claim: The TSS of heat shock protein genes opens substantially by 30 min in response to heat.
source: This is in contrast to the TSS of heat shock protein genes (HSPs), which possesses less accessible chromatin than that of ARGs at baseline but opens substantially by 30 min in both the dTrpA1 and control flies in response to heat (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C using ATAC-seq data.

claim: The whole gene body of heat shock genes opens with heat.
source: In fact, the whole gene body of heat shock genes opens with heat, consistent with what was shown previously at the hsp70 locus (Petesch and Lis, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data and a citation to Petesch and Lis, 2008.

claim: ARG TSSs are notably more accessible prior to stimulation compared to all expressed, annotated genes.
source: Despite the lack of a firing-induced change in ARG chromatin TSSs (Figure 6A), they are notably more accessible prior to stimulation compared to all expressed, annotated genes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D using ATAC-seq data.

claim: Only KCl-induced ARGs show significantly higher baseline expression levels.
source: This is unlikely due to higher baseline expression levels; only KCl-induced ARGs show significantly higher baseline expression levels despite showing intermediate chromatin accessibility of the three firing paradigms (Figure 6—figure supplements 3, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lola binding sites are enriched in ChR2-XXL-induced ARGs with significance = 4.13E-07.
source: Lola (significance = 4.13E-07), eip78C (significance = 5.92E-05), relish (rel, significance = 1.78E-04), broad (br, significance = 6.62E-02, insignificant) and cf2 (significance = 0.43, insignificant) were chosen to represent different levels of enrichment ranking, from high to low (Figure 7—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on motif enrichment analysis.

claim: eip78C binding sites are enriched in ChR2-XXL-induced ARGs with significance = 5.92E-05.
source: Lola (significance = 4.13E-07), eip78C (significance = 5.92E-05), relish (rel, significance = 1.78E-04), broad (br, significance = 6.62E-02, insignificant) and cf2 (significance = 0.43, insignificant) were chosen to represent different levels of enrichment ranking, from high to low (Figure 7—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on motif enrichment analysis.

claim: relish binding sites are enriched in ChR2-XXL-induced ARGs with significance = 1.78E-04.
source: Lola (significance = 4.13E-07), eip78C (significance = 5.92E-05), relish (rel, significance = 1.78E-04), broad (br, significance = 6.62E-02, insignificant) and cf2 (significance = 0.43, insignificant) were chosen to represent different levels of enrichment ranking, from high to low (Figure 7—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on motif enrichment analysis.

claim: The three transcription factors (LOLA, EIP78C, and REL) with high significance showed a dramatic increase in luciferase signal immediately after LED exposure.
source: The three transcription factors (LOLA, EIP78C, and REL) with high significance showed a dramatic increase in luciferase signal immediately after LED exposure, and the signal decayed in about an hour (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The luciferase signal from LOLA, EIP78C, and REL reporters decayed in about an hour.
source: The three transcription factors (LOLA, EIP78C, and REL) with high significance showed a dramatic increase in luciferase signal immediately after LED exposure, and the signal decayed in about an hour (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The two transcription factors with much lower significance (br, cf2) showed no change in luciferase signal.
source: In contrast, the two transcription factors with much lower significance (br, cf2) showed no change (Figure 7—figure supplement 1.).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fly ARGs vary with the individual stimulation paradigm.
source: Fly ARGs vary with the individual stimulation paradigm and are surprisingly cell type-specific.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Fly ARGs are surprisingly cell type-specific.
source: Fly ARGs vary with the individual stimulation paradigm and are surprisingly cell type-specific.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data in Figure 5.

claim: Fly ARGs are more functionally diverse compared to mammalian ARGs.
source: Fly ARGs are also more functionally diverse and have longer gene lengths compared to mammalian ARGs.
evidence: This is based on the GO analysis showing weak enrichment and comparison with mammalian literature.

claim: Fly ARGs have longer gene lengths compared to mammalian ARGs.
source: Fly ARGs are also more functionally diverse and have longer gene lengths compared to mammalian ARGs.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 2C and comparisons with mammalian gene lengths.

claim: Chromatin at TSS of fly ARGs is more accessible at baseline than other expressed genes.
source: Chromatin at transcription start sites (TSS) of fly ARGs is more accessible at baseline than other expressed genes but does not change with stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by the ATAC-seq data in Figure 6D.

claim: Chromatin at TSS of fly ARGs does not change with stimulation.
source: Chromatin at transcription start sites (TSS) of fly ARGs is more accessible at baseline than other expressed genes but does not change with stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by the ATAC-seq data in Figure 6A.

claim: Mammalian IEGs are largely shared between different types of neurons such as excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Mammalian IEGs are largely shared between different types of neurons such as excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Spiegel et al., 2014), but fly ARGs like SRGs appear quite tissue-type specific, i.e., many genes are only induced in one of the tissue types tested despite similar baseline levels (Figure 5) (Mardinly et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Spiegel et al., 2014.

claim: Fly ARGs like SRGs appear quite tissue-type specific.
source: Mammalian IEGs are largely shared between different types of neurons such as excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Spiegel et al., 2014), but fly ARGs like SRGs appear quite tissue-type specific, i.e., many genes are only induced in one of the tissue types tested despite similar baseline levels (Figure 5) (Mardinly et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5 and a citation to Mardinly et al., 2016.

claim: Fly neurons appear quite heterogeneous with distinct transcript enrichment and electrophysiological properties.
source: This is in line with the fact that fly neurons appear quite heterogeneous, e.g., they have distinct transcript enrichment and electrophysiological properties (Liang et al., 2016; Nagoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2016 and Nagoshi et al., 2010.

claim: The PDF cell-ARGs are a subset of the mRNAs that undergo circadian oscillations within these neurons.
source: As an example, preliminary analysis indicates that the PDF cell-ARGs are a subset of the mRNAs that undergo circadian oscillations within these neurons ([Kula-Eversole et al., 2010] and data not shown).
evidence: This is based on preliminary analysis and a citation to Kula-Eversole et al., 2010.

claim: Induction of IEGs like fos and egr1 was observed in birds and zebrafish but with smaller increases (about 4 to 6-fold) than human and mice (usually well above 10-fold).
source: For example, induction of IEGs like fos and egr1 was also observed in birds and zebrafish but with smaller increases (about 4 to 6-fold) than human and mice (usually well above 10-fold) (Bébien et al., 2003; Burmeister and Fernald, 2005; Lopes et al., 2015; Mokin and Keifer, 2005; Moore and Whitmore, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Mammals may need a more potent initial transcriptional system than flies to respond to firing.
source: In any case, one can imagine that mammals need a more potent initial transcriptional system than flies to respond to firing.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the differences observed.

claim: Mammalian neurons are bigger with more and longer processes than fly neurons.
source: Not only are mammalian neurons bigger with more and longer processes, but they also have much larger genomes (longer genomic DNA and more enhancers to bind); both of these factors may require higher levels of transcripts to generate a required higher abundance of transcription factors.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about neuronal anatomy.

claim: Mammals have much larger genomes than flies with longer genomic DNA and more enhancers.
source: Not only are mammalian neurons bigger with more and longer processes, but they also have much larger genomes (longer genomic DNA and more enhancers to bind); both of these factors may require higher levels of transcripts to generate a required higher abundance of transcription factors.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about genome sizes.

claim: Histones around IEG promoters in mammals are modified to be more accessible to transcription factors at baseline.
source: In the cases of mammals, histones around IEGs promoters are modified to be more accessible to transcription factors at baseline; the modification levels could be even higher with firing (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2010.

claim: The modification levels of histones around IEG promoters could be even higher with firing in mammals.
source: In the cases of mammals, histones around IEGs promoters are modified to be more accessible to transcription factors at baseline; the modification levels could be even higher with firing (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2010.
